metadata.methods_description: Simultaneous EEG, ESG, ENG and EMG were recorded, along with ECG and respiration, during rest with eyes open and during mixed median nerve, tibial nerve, and alternating median/tibial nerve stimulation. The EEG channel Fz was referenced to the right mastoid and, separately, to the 6th thoracic vertebra (TH6) for ESG. Data are in EEGLAB format organized per BIDS.

citation_details.title: Evaluating cardiac noise correction approaches for non-invasive electrophysiology of the human spinal cord
citation_details.author: Emma Bailey, Birgit Nierula, Tilman Stephani, Burkhard Maeß, Vadim V. Nikulin, Falk Eippert
citation_details.abstract: The spinal cord is an important component of the central nervous system for the processing of sensorimotor information transmitted between the body and the brain. Electrospinography (ESG) is the most accessible non-invasive technique for recording spinal signals in humans, but the detrimental impact of physiological noise (mostly of cardiac nature) has prevented widespread adoption. Here, we aim to address this issue by examining various denoising algorithms for cardiac artefact reduction-including approaches based on principal component analysis (PCA), independent component analysis (ICA), signal space projection (SSP), canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and denoising separation of sources (DSS). We observed that in situations where large number of spinal electrodes are used, ICA and SSP offer the best results in terms of balancing the removal of noise and preserving neural information of interest. In cases where only a small number of electrodes are available, an approach based on PCA is deemed helpful. Finally, we also approached this issue from a signal-enhancement perspective by applying CCA and DSS directly to signals of interest, namely spinal somatosensory evoked potentials (SEPs, especially the N13 and N22 components in the cervical and lumbar spinal cord, respectively). We observed that in cases where extensive electrode arrays are used in the context of task-based designs, CCA reveals clear evoked spinal potentials even with single-trial resolution. Taken together, there are several appropriate algorithms for physiological noise removal and/or signal enhancement in ESG, rendering this an accessible and easy-to-use technique for non-invasive assessments of human spinal cord function.

citation_details.title: A Cascade Spatial-Temporal Denoising Strategy for Cardiac Artifact Removal in Spinal Cord Electrophysiology: A Pilot Study
citation_details.author: Baole Zeng
citation_details.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
citation_details.abstract: Background: Cardiac electrical activity introduces severe artifacts in spinal cord electrophysiology (ESG), masking the subtle neural signals. Traditional methods, such as Spatial Signal Projection (SSP) and Adaptive Template Subtraction (ATS), are often used individually but have inherent limitations. Objective: This study aims to evaluate whether a cascade strategy (SSP followed by ATS) can suppress cardiac artifacts while preserving spinal SEPs in a representative single-subject control, and to quantify any suppression–preservation trade-off. Methods: Raw ESG data from five subjects were obtained from the OpenNeuro public dataset (ds004388). The data included tibial and median nerve stimulation tasks, resulting in a total of 234 channel-task pairs. The proposed cascade strategy was compared against standalone SSP and ATS. The Residual Index (RI) metric was used to quantify denoising performance. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Linear Mixed-Effects Models (LMM) were performed for statistical analysis. Results: The cascade strategy achieved the lowest RI across 116 out of 117 channel-task pairs (99.1%) in the tibial task and 116 out of 117 channel-task pairs (99.1%) in the median task. Wilcoxon tests showed significant improvement over both SSP and ATS (both p < 0.001); LMM sensitivity analysis was consistent with superiority over ATS (p < 0.001) and SSP (p < 0.05). In a single-subject median-task control (sub-001), an order-reversal control showed no difference in RI between SSP→ATS and ATS→SSP. However, SEP retention analysis revealed a substantial trade-off in ESG channels (cascade median 9.29% in the 38 analyzed ESG channels of sub-001). Conclusion: The cascade strategy provides the strongest cardiac artifact suppression among the compared methods, but at the cost of substantial SEP attenuation in ESG channels in the analyzed subset. This trade-off highlights a critical challenge for linear denoising in ESG and suggests that future BSI decoding pipelines should prioritize methods that explicitly preserve stimulus-locked spinal responses.

citation_details.title: Non-invasive electrophysiology across the human central nervous system
citation_details.author: Emma Bailey
citation_details.venue: Qucosa (Saxon State and University Library Dresden)
citation_details.abstract: The spinal cord, despite its central role in sensory and motor integration, remains under investigated compared to the brain. This thesis first addresses key obstacles to non‑invasive electrophysiological recordings from the human spinal cord by developing optimal strategies for removing large cardiac artefacts in electrospinography (ESG) data, markedly enhancing signal quality. Using these refined methods, electroencephalography (EEG) was then combined with simultaneous ESG as a tool to probe entire human central nervous system (CNS) function, investigating both evoked and intrinsic neural activity. Together, these studies strengthen the usability of ESG, reveal novel features of CNS dynamics, and underscore the potential of spinal cord electrophysiology in both basic and clinical research.
